title: The Feather review and being recognized as one gets older
summary: Feather's grand marshal remark leads Royal to say recognition comes when you are less competitive.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Being honored: NEA Jazz Masters and other awards

blocks.x: Yes. I wanted to get into the record a funny thing from Leonard Feather's review of your concert with Nat Pierce and Frankie Capp, last Sunday (inaudible) Frank Katt (PHONETIC), in which he referred to you as "the grand Marshal of the alto saxophone, Marshal Royal, romantically showcased in Benny Carter's "A Souvenir," (inaudible) which was kind of nice. To go from being called a "valuable general" from the British book to the newspaper that called you the "grand Marshal of the alto saxophone."
Well, there are certain things that only happen to you after you have become a certain age. So

now, I'm probably being recognized strictly because I am less competitive probably than I was as a younger fella. When it gets to the place where you are less competitive, then people will start recognizing you for what you are, just the same as they do people when they die. That's when they write beautiful eulogies about them and tell them how beautiful and how wonderful they are. But at the present time, I'm not quite as competitive as I was 25 or 30 years ago. That's strictly to my own choosing, because that's the way I want it to be.
I don't want to be competitive. I want to live cool.
Well, yes, but any comment on your playing now should be inspired inscribed by your playing and your playing is beautiful.
Now, or any of the times I've ever heard it (inaudible).

Well, actually, how well you play and how much you're respected for your playing and the acclaim that you can get out of it is a different thing altogether. There are a whole lot of reasons sometimes why people don't give you the acclaim that is supposed to be given you, but if you're not able to accept their -- it's not always a denial. It's a matter of a person not even recognizing you and when you don't get recognition, that is when it's there. A person can say something bad about your playing and you can improve upon it if it is truthful. But if you're just sort of sit over in a corner
and ignored, and not recognized, well, then, that's the worst part of -- any part of being an artist. Because frustration can be very, very humiliating.
